title: Derivative
body:
[[Chain Rule]]

---

$$
f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}
$$

The derivative is the **slope of the tangent line**, defined as a [[Limit]] of slopes of secant
lines. Pick a second point $h$ away, compute rise over run, then slide the second point into the
first. The quotient is $0/0$ at $h = 0$, which is exactly why it has to be a limit and not an
evaluation.

```
    secant through (x, f(x)) and (x+h, f(x+h))

    f(x+h) - f(x)        as h → 0 the secant pivots
    -------------        down onto the tangent at x
          h
```

## Three readings of one number

| Reading | Question it answers | Where it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| **slope** | how steep is the curve here | [[Curve Sketching]], tangent lines |
| **instantaneous rate of change** | how fast is this changing right now | [[Related Rates]], velocity from position |
| **sensitivity** | if I nudge the input, how much does the output move | [[Gradient Descent]], error propagation |

The third is the one that matters for CS. "Which way should I move $x$ to make $f(x)$ smaller, and
how much does moving help" is a question about $f'$, and it is the whole of
[[Optimization]] and of training a [[Neural Network]].

## Notation

$f'(x)$, $\frac{dy}{dx}$, $\frac{d}{dx}f(x)$, and $\dot{y}$ all mean the same thing. Leibniz's
$\frac{dy}{dx}$ is worth preferring when the [[Chain Rule]] or [[Related Rates]] are involved,
because it names both variables and the cancellation pattern $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\cdot
\frac{du}{dx}$ then looks like arithmetic. It is not actually a fraction, but
[[Linear Approximation]] explains why it behaves like one.

Higher derivatives: $f''$ is the derivative of $f'$, the rate at which the rate is changing.
Position, velocity, acceleration is the same ladder.

## When it fails to exist

Differentiable requires the limit to exist from both sides, so it fails at corners ($|x|$ at $0$),
cusps, vertical tangents, and anywhere the function is not [[Continuity|continuous]]. Hence the
one-way implication: **differentiable $\Rightarrow$ continuous, never the reverse.**

## Computing them

Nobody uses the limit definition after the first week. [[Differentiation Rules]] holds the table,
[[Chain Rule]] handles compositions, and [[Implicit Differentiation]] handles equations that were
never solved for $y$.
